title: Honest citizenship
hookLine: Sikhs take part honestly in the life of their countries

lines: A JURY SUMMONS, A FORM, A BALLOT.
cards: A jury summons arrives in a plain envelope, and the first thought is how to get out of it. A form asks you to report every bit of income, and there's a small line you could leave blank.
A ballot sits on the counter for a week. Nobody will make a film about filling in a form truthfully.
But this is where a lot of public life actually happens: small, boring moments where honesty costs a little and nobody's watching.
Sikh teaching has something to say about them, and it starts with a line that ranks something above truth itself.

teach.b: First, the line. In Sri Raag, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: truth is higher than everything, but higher still is truthful living. Not just believing what's true; living it, in the dull places.
A truthful life includes the tax form. Second, kirat. Sikh teaching asks for an honest living, kirat karni.
In a hymn in Raag Sarang, Guru Nanak says the one who eats what they've earned by their own effort, and gives some of it away with their own hand, knows the way.
Earn honestly, share freely: a good neighbor and a good citizen in one sentence. Third, wherever they live.

Sikhs live in many places and take part in public life in many ways: as soldiers and nurses, teachers and drivers, voters and volunteers. You may have seen Sikh volunteers cooking for strangers after a storm or a flood.
That's langar leaving the gurdwara and walking into the street. Faith here isn't kept apart from the town; it's how you show up in it. Fourth, the small duties.

teach.h: THE FORM, THE SUMMONS, THE BALLOT.
teach.b: Answering the summons. Filling the form truthfully. Paying the fine you actually owe.
Voting, or helping someone get to the polls. Picking up the litter outside your own door. None of these is a sermon.
Each one is truthful living, the thing Guru Nanak placed higher still, tested at the kitchen counter, not the podium.

how: Sikhs speak of kirat karni, earning an honest living, and of seva beyond the gurdwara, which can mean volunteering, serving food in times of need, and taking part in the life of their towns and countries.

o: truthful living carried into everyday public duties
obeying every law without ever questioning it
joining a political party to serve your faith

p: earn by effort, give with your hand
cooking for strangers after a storm

s: in Sikh teaching, believing the truth is enough
Guru Nanak says truthful living is higher still.
Guru Nanak praises the one who earns by effort and shares
in Raag Sarang: eat what you earn, give some with your hand.
honest citizenship is mostly about big public gestures
it's mostly small duties done fully: the form, the summons, the ballot.

games.q: you're filling in a form, and there's a line you could leave blank and nobody would ever know. what does truthful living ask?
o: ask a friend whether anyone checks.
games.why: Guru Nanak places truthful living above truth alone, and that includes the parts nobody checks.

practice: Let the small public things you've been putting off run past, a form, a bill, a neighbor's request, a broken streetlight to report, and let one rise to the top.
Breathe in and admit, honestly and without blame, why you've avoided it. Breathe out and picture yourself doing it fully, even the part nobody would check.

wordCard.voice: Honest citizenship. Truthful living, which Guru Nanak placed higher than truth alone, carried into the form, the summons and the street. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kirat, honest work; kirat karni is earning a living honestly.

carryVoice: Your line: honest citizens. Langar walks out of the gurdwara and into the street. Rest well.

sources.ref: Ang 62 (Sri Raag, Guru Nanak: sachahu orai sabh ko upar sach achar)
Ang 1245 (Var Sarang, salok of Guru Nanak: ghal khai kichh hathhu dei)
